extracted.subtask_description: The 61st William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition problem set (A–1 through A–6 and B–1 through B–6), a collection of undergraduate-level contest problems requiring proofs or constructions. Useful as tasks for problem-solving practice or as targets for worked solutions and explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: A-1
rubrics_metrics.description: Let A be a positive real number. What are the possible values of Σ_{j=0}^∞ x_j^2, given that x_0, x_1, ... are positive numbers for which Σ_{j=0}^∞ x_j = A?

rubrics_metrics.name: A-2
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove that there exist infinitely many integers n such that n, n+1, n+2 are each the sum of the squares of two integers. [Example: 0 = 0^2 + 0^2, 1 = 0^2 + 1^2, 2 = 1^2 + 1^2.]

rubrics_metrics.name: A-3
rubrics_metrics.description: The octagon P1P2P3P4P5P6P7P8 is inscribed in a circle, with the vertices around the circumference in the given order. Given that the polygon P1P3P5P7 is a square of area 5, and the polygon P2P4P6P8 is a rectangle of area 4, find the maximum possible area of the octagon.

rubrics_metrics.name: A-4
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that the improper integral lim_{B→∞} ∫_0^B sin(x) sin(x^2) dx converges.

rubrics_metrics.name: A-5
rubrics_metrics.description: Three distinct points with integer coordinates lie in the plane on a circle of radius r > 0. Show that two of these points are separated by a distance of at least r^{1/3}.

rubrics_metrics.name: A-6
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f(x) be a polynomial with integer coefficients. Define a sequence a_0, a_1, ... of integers such that a_0 = 0 and a_{n+1} = f(a_n) for all n ≥ 0. Prove that if there exists a positive integer m for which a_m = 0 then either a_1 = 0 or a_2 = 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: B-1
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a_j, b_j, c_j be integers for 1 ≤ j ≤ N. Assume for each j, at least one of a_j, b_j, c_j is odd. Show that there exist integers r, s, t such that r a_j + s b_j + t c_j is odd for at least 4N/7 values of j, 1 ≤ j ≤ N.

rubrics_metrics.name: B-3
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f(t) = Σ_{j=1}^N a_j sin(2π j t), where each a_j is real and a_N ≠ 0. Let N_k denote the number of zeroes (including multiplicities) of d^k f / dt^k. Prove that N_0 ≤ N_1 ≤ N_2 ≤ ··· and lim_{k→∞} N_k = 2N. [Editorial clarification: only zeroes in [0,1) should be counted.]

rubrics_metrics.name: B-4
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f(x) be a continuous function such that f(2x^2 − 1) = 2x f(x) for all x. Show that f(x) = 0 for −1 ≤ x ≤ 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: B-5
rubrics_metrics.description: Let S_0 be a finite set of positive integers. We define finite sets S_1, S_2, ... of positive integers as follows: the integer a is in S_{n+1} if and only if exactly one of a−1 or a is in S_n. Show that there exist infinitely many integers N for which S_N = S_0 ∪ {N + a : a ∈ S_0}.

rubrics_metrics.name: B-6
rubrics_metrics.description: Let B be a set of more than 2^n + 1/n distinct points with coordinates of the form (±1, ±1, ..., ±1) in n-dimensional space with n ≥ 3. Show that there are three distinct points in B which are the vertices of an equilateral triangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PDF extraction shows 'more than 2n+1/n' which appears to be a rendering artifact; the intended Putnam statement involves a bound on the number of points of the n-dimensional ±1-cube. The core requirement is to prove existence of an equilateral triangle among sufficiently many ±1-vertices when n ≥ 3.
